source_text: Ἐγὼ δὲ εὖ οἶδα, ὡς οὔτε οἱ κουφότατοι δοκοῦντες τὸν μέγαν δρόμον ἐκεῖνον ἀνύσουσιν, οὔτε οἱ δυνατοὶ καὶ φοβεροὶ παρὰ ἀνθρώποις δεδοξασμένοι, τὸν φοβερὸν πόλεμον νικήσουσιν. Ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ ἐν ἐδωδῆς πλήθει φρόνησις δοκιμάζεται, οὐδὲ σύνεσις πλούτῳ κοινωνεῖν εἴωθεν. Οὐδὲ συγχαίρω τοῖς οἰομένοις ἅπαντας τῶν ὁμοίων τεύξεσθαι. Πάνυ δὲ ὑπνώττειν ἐοίκασιν οἱ τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐνθυμούμενοι, καὶ μὴ λογιζόμενοι, ὡς δίκην ἰχθύων καὶ ὀρνέων ἀνάρπαστοι γινόμενοι, ἐν κακοῖς κατατριβήσονται, ἄφνω τῆς ἀξίας λαχόντες ἐπιτιμίας. Ἐγὼ δὲ σοφίαν οὕτω τι μέγα ἡγοῦμαι, ὡς καὶ πόλιν μικρὰν ὑπ᾽ ὀλίγων μὲν οἰκουμένην, ὑπὸ δὲ μεγάλου πολιορκουμένην βασιλέως χειρὶ, πολλὴν καὶ μεγάλην ἡγοῦμαι, εἰ καὶ ἕνα σοφὸν ἄνδρα πολίτην ἔχοι πένητα. Δύναιτο γὰρ ἂν οὗτος καὶ ἐκ τῶν πολεμίων, καὶ ἐκ τῶν χαρακωμάτων τὴν ἑαυτοῦ διασῶσαι πόλιν. Καὶ ἄλλοι μὲν τὸν σοφὸν ἐκεῖνον οὐ γινώσκουσι πένητα· ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ πάνυ προκρίνω τὴν ἐν σοφίᾳ ἰσχὺν ταύτης τῆς δημώδους δυνάμεως. Ἀλλ᾽ ἐνθάδε μὲν ἀτιμάζεται σοφία πενίᾳ συνοικοῦσα· ἀκουσθήσεται δὲ μετέπειτα ὑπερφωνοῦσα δυνάστας καὶ τυράννους κακῶν ὀρεγομένους. Σοφία γὰρ καὶ σιδήρου δυνατωτέρα· Ἀφροσύνη τε ἑνὸς πολλοῖς κίνδυνον ἐργάζεται, κἂν πολλοῖς καταφρόνητος ᾖ.
thought_title: The poor wise man who could save a city
orientation: Wisdom outweighs strength and wealth: one poor wise man could save a besieged city.
pass_a_gloss: I well know that neither the ones seeming lightest/swiftest will accomplish that great race, nor the powerful and fearsome esteemed among men will conquer the fearful war. But neither in abundance of food is prudence tested, nor is understanding accustomed to share with wealth. Nor do I rejoice with those supposing all will obtain the same things. Very much asleep seem those pondering such things, and not reckoning that, like fish and birds becoming snatched away, they will be worn away in evils, suddenly obtaining by lot the deserved penalty. I consider wisdom so great a thing that even a small city, inhabited by few, besieged by the hand of a great king, I consider much and great, if it has even one wise man as citizen, poor. For this man could save his own city both from the enemies and from the palisades/siege works. And others do not know that wise man, poor; but I very much prefer the strength in wisdom to this popular power. But here wisdom cohabiting with poverty is dishonored; yet it will be heard afterward, outshouting dynasts and tyrants reaching for evils. For wisdom is more powerful even than iron; and folly of one works danger for many, even if it (folly) be despised by many.

pass_b_english: But I know well that those who seem swiftest will not finish that great race, and those reputed among men as mighty and fearsome will not win the fearful war; nor is prudence proved by an abundance of food, nor does understanding usually keep company with wealth (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Nor do I share the gladness of those who think that all people will meet the same lot (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Those who ponder such things seem to be fast asleep. They do not reckon that, snatched away like fish and birds, they will be worn down in misfortunes, suddenly receiving the penalty they deserve (Ecclesiastes 9:12).

But I hold wisdom so great a thing that even a small city, inhabited by few and besieged by the hand of a great king, I count populous and great if it has even one wise citizen, though he is poor (Ecclesiastes 9:13–15). For such a man could save his own city both from the enemy and from the siege works. Others do not recognize that poor wise man (Ecclesiastes 9:15); but I much prefer the strength that lies in wisdom to this common sort of power (Ecclesiastes 9:16). Here, it is true, wisdom that lives with poverty is held in dishonor (Ecclesiastes 9:16); but afterward it will be heard, its voice rising above rulers and tyrants who reach for evil (Ecclesiastes 9:17). For wisdom is stronger even than iron; and the folly of one man brings danger on many, even if many despise it (Ecclesiastes 9:18).
notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 9:11-18. 'That great race' keeps the demonstrative ἐκεῖνον; 'the fearful war' has none. 'Nor is prudence proved by a great deal of food' renders ἐν ἐδωδῆς πλήθει, Gregory's turn on 'bread to the wise' (Ecclesiastes 9:11). The sentence about those who think all meet the same lot recasts Ecclesiastes 9:11b ('time and chance happen to them all') by rejecting it; cited to that verse because it is Gregory's rendering of it. 'Others do not recognize' renders οὐ γινώσκουσι (Ecclesiastes 9:15 has 'no one remembered'). 'Its voice rising above' renders ὑπερφωνοῦσα (literally 'outshouting'). No Psalm citations, so no renumbering. 'I hold wisdom so great a thing' renders Ecclesiastes 9:13 ('this wisdom seemed great to me'), so that citation runs 9:13-15 (the 1622 Latin also starts verse 13 here). 'This common sort of power' renders ταύτης τῆς δημώδους δυνάμεως. 'Even if many despise it' takes folly (ἀφροσύνη) as the subject of κἂν ... ᾖ, as the 1622 Latin does ('etiamsi multis leuis & contemptibilis sit').
